# Harden your service & control access {#sec-lab-07 .unnumbered}

*Exercise 7 · Session 7 lab · Estimated time: 90-120 min*

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
This is the practical task for [Chapter 7: Hardening and access control](../chapters/07-hardening-access-control.qmd).
Work through it in your lab group; you talk your answers through at the
session after next (the review runs one session behind). **This page
mirrors the worksheet for reading and reference - the official worksheet
is the PDF distributed via Canvas.**
:::

Write your answers in the answer document `SKY2100_Exercise7_Answers.docx`. Last week you put Nextcloud behind HTTPS. The service is
encrypted but still exposed: default settings, an open SSH port, a single admin account. Today you
*shrink the attack surface* and decide *who* may get in. You will reduce running services,
lock down the firewall and SSH, add brute-force protection, and apply least privilege inside the app.

::: {.callout-warning title="Caution"}
Work only on your *own* VM. Before you disable SSH password login,
make sure key-based login already works in a second terminal - so you cannot lock yourself out.
:::

## Map the attack surface

- [ ] **List everything that is listening on your VM and who owns each port:**

  ```bash
  ss -tulpn
  ```

- [ ] **Which ports are exposed, and which do you actually need for an HTTPS Nextcloud you administer over SSH? Mark any you can switch off.**

## Default-deny firewall (UFW)

- [ ] **Configure UFW to deny everything inbound, then allow only what you need:**

  ```bash
  sudo ufw --force reset   # start clean: the S4 rules (22 and 80 open to all) would otherwise stay
  sudo ufw default deny incoming
  sudo ufw default allow outgoing
  sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
  sudo ufw allow from <your-ip> to any port 22
  sudo ufw enable && sudo ufw status verbose
  ```

- [ ] **Why is "default deny, then allow" safer than "allow the bad ports"? (one or two lines)**

## Harden SSH

- [ ] **Set up key-based login (if not already), then in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` set:**

  ```
  PasswordAuthentication no
  PermitRootLogin no
  ```

  Reload with `sudo systemctl reload ssh`. **Keep your current session open** and confirm a new
  key-based login works before closing it.
- [ ] **Why disable password authentication and root login specifically? Link each to a threat.**

## Brute-force protection (fail2ban)

- [ ] **Install and enable fail2ban for SSH:**

  ```bash
  sudo apt install -y fail2ban
  sudo systemctl enable --now fail2ban
  sudo fail2ban-client status sshd
  ```

- [ ] **Trigger a few failed logins from another machine/IP, then check the jail again. What changed?**

## Least privilege inside the app

- [ ] **In Nextcloud, create a *non-admin* user and give it only the access it needs. Do *not* use the admin account for everyday work.**
- [ ] **Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) on the admin account.**
- [ ] **State one thing the admin can do that your new user cannot - and why that is least privilege.**

## Cloud transfer: Microsoft Learn

- [ ] **Work through "Secure your Azure resources with Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)".**

  [learn.microsoft.com/training/modules/secure-azure-resources-with-rbac](https://learn.microsoft.com/training/modules/secure-azure-resources-with-rbac/)
- [ ] **In Azure RBAC you assign a role to an identity at a scope. Name the four scope levels from broadest to narrowest, and say which you would choose for least privilege.**

## Azure reflection

- [ ] **Your UFW rules protect one VM. Which Azure construct enforces the *same* default-deny idea across your cloud resources, and at which layer (host vs. network)?**
- [ ] **CSA calls IAM "the new perimeter". In your own words, why does identity matter *more* in the cloud than the network perimeter did on-premises?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Aha"}
Last week the service was encrypted, yet today you still had work to do: an open SSH port, a single
all-powerful admin, default settings. Encryption did not make the service safe, because reachability and
access are separate problems from confidentiality on the wire. Notice where the real boundary sits now.
On-premises you could draw a line around the building and trust what was inside, but your cloud service
has no inside; anyone who reaches it is judged by who they are, not where they connect from. That is why
identity is the new perimeter, and why least privilege, MFA and a locked-down SSH matter more than any
network wall.
:::

## Knowledge check

1. Define **attack surface** and give two ways hardening reduces it.

   **Hint:** Every point an attacker could enter or extract data - hardening shrinks it.
2. Why can a cloud tenant *not* rely on traditional perimeter security? (Comer)

   **Hint:** You share physical servers and links with other tenants - no hard perimeter.
3. State the difference between **authentication** and **authorisation**.

   **Hint:** One proves who you are; one decides what you may do.
4. Name the three authentication factors and say what **MFA** combines.

   **Hint:** Something you know, have, are - and combining two different ones.
5. Distinguish **RBAC** from **ABAC** with one example each.

   **Hint:** Permissions by role, versus permissions by attributes and conditions.
6. State the **principle of least privilege** in one sentence.

   **Hint:** The minimum access an identity needs, and nothing more.
7. CSA defines an **entitlement** as a rule over which four things?

   **Hint:** A rule: which entity, which actions, which resources, under which conditions.
8. What does **zero trust** mean for how each request is handled?

   **Hint:** Trust nothing by default; verify every request instead of a one-time gate.
9. What is **single sign-on (SSO)**, and what problem does it solve?

   **Hint:** One login across services from a central identity system - no password sprawl.
10. What is **PAM**, and why are privileged accounts treated specially?

    **Hint:** Identity for admin accounts, which can do the most damage if taken.
11. In Azure RBAC, what three things make up a role assignment?

    **Hint:** Identity, role, and the scope it applies to.
12. Name two **common cloud access-control mistakes** and the fix for each.

    **Hint:** Admin roles without MFA, long-lived static keys, over-broad roles.
